channel.title: DE//AGENT — Learn the pattern. Install the skill. Run the pipeline.
channel.description: An open registry and learning platform for modern Data Engineering: tutorials, architecture patterns, agent skills, MCP servers, agents, hooks and production runbooks — each with provenance, license, compatibility and verification status.

item.title: Catalogs and ownership: who owns this table and is it safe to use?
item.description: Every incident resolves faster when you can ask a catalog what this data is, who owns it, and whether it is safe to use. Run the catalog-assistant workflow end to end — resolve, retrieve, summarise — and keep it read-only and metadata-only by design.

item.title: Express a freshness check as a metric and an alert
item.description: The first hands-on of the series: declare a freshness SLA, express staleness as a metric, and write an alert rule — including what happens when no data arrives at all. Ends with the pre-merge check that keeps schedules honest against the SLA they claim.

item.title: Hold the observability mental model: infrastructure metrics versus data signals
item.description: Two layers live on one data platform: infrastructure metrics (CPU, lag, job success) and data signals (freshness, volume, schema, distribution). This lesson separates them, places lineage and catalogs on the map, and names the four data signals every pipeline owes you before you write a dashboard.

item.title: Hold the row-versus-column mental model
item.description: Before you pick a file format, understand why analytics engines read columnar files at all: row groups carrying min/max statistics let a reader prune most of the file before decoding it, and columnar layout means a scan of three columns never touches the other twenty. Every later lesson in this series builds on this model.

item.title: Hold the system design mental model — data systems as tradeoffs
item.description: Before any diagram, data systems are tradeoffs, not products. This lesson fixes the vocabulary — reliability, scalability, maintainability, and the six canonical mechanisms behind them — and shows how the canonical chapters map onto systems you already run, so every later lesson in the series has a place to land.

item.title: Open the Parquet file — row groups, pages, encodings
item.description: A Parquet file is not a black box — it is row groups of column chunks made of pages, with statistics that readers use for predicate pushdown. Learn the anatomy from the two Parquet sources and you can reason about every read and every layout decision later in this series.

item.title: Run the back-of-envelope drill — numbers before architecture
item.description: Estimation is the warm-up act of every design conversation: QPS, storage per day, retention, peak factor, all written down before a single box is drawn. This lesson drills the powers-of-two arithmetic and shows how to ground the numbers in architectures that actually ship.

item.title: The twelve-factor vocabulary for pipeline jobs
item.description: Data pipelines run as jobs on shared infrastructure, so the twelve-factor principles apply to them — config in the environment, backing services as attached resources, logs as event streams, disposability, and dev/prod parity. Learn the vocabulary engineers already share when arguing about config, logs, and process design.

item.title: Arrow — columnar memory and zero-copy interchange
item.description: Between the file on disk and the engine doing work sits memory. Apache Arrow defines the columnar in-memory format, its language bindings, the IPC and Flight protocols, and zero-copy interchange between systems — which is why modern data tools can hand columns to each other without re-serializing everything in between.

item.title: Avro and schema evolution for event payloads
item.description: Event payloads change while consumers keep running. Avro's answer is a schema declared next to the data, evolution rules carried by the schema registry, and a container format used across event and stream pipelines. Walk the Avro docs' own four topics and see where the format sits against Parquet and Arrow.

item.title: Capstone — the foundations checklist
item.description: Ten lessons compress into one checklist — place every decision on the lifecycle, lay out analytics files with row groups and statistics, expect Arrow at the boundaries, evolve event payloads with Avro's rules, and run jobs twelve-factor style. Each line cites the source that owns the claim.

item.title: Capstone: the data-platform observability checklist
item.description: Ten lessons compress into one page. Declare SLAs, express them as metrics and alerts with explicit no-data handling, instrument runs with traces, emit lineage events, keep the catalog authoritative — and gate both schedule changes and column changes pre-merge.

item.title: Choose storage engines on tradeoffs — reads, writes, and consistency
item.description: Storage choice is where a design's promises become real: the engine you pick decides what replication buys, what partitioning costs, and which consistency semantics your merges get. This lesson builds a decision habit around the DDIA mechanisms instead of brand loyalty.

item.title: Choosing file formats — Parquet, Avro, and Arrow's role
item.description: The three formats in this series are not competitors — they answer different questions. Parquet is the columnar file for analytics scans, Avro is the schema-evolving container for event payloads, and Arrow is the in-memory substrate between systems. Make the comparison explicit so the next format debate takes minutes, not days.

item.title: Column-level lineage: the concepts and the event standard
item.description: Table-level lineage says a job touched a table; column-level lineage says which columns feed which. Learn the concepts, the OpenLineage event model that makes lineage work across tools, and how an impact set is computed from a lineage store.

item.title: Compression and encodings — the tradeoffs behind the file
item.description: Encodings and compression codecs are where file size and scan speed are actually decided — Parquet applies encodings and codecs per column chunk with statistics on top, while Avro carries schema plus encoding for event payloads. Learn what each layer buys you before you pick defaults.

item.title: Define reliability in numbers — SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets
item.description: A design without reliability numbers is a wish. This lesson borrows the SRE toolkit — SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, incident management, postmortems, and capacity planning — and points it at data platforms, where freshness and completeness are the properties users actually feel.

item.title: Design resilient pipelines — retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead
item.description: Failures are inputs, not exceptions. Microsoft's pattern catalogue gives each failure shape a name and a solution — retry, circuit breaker, compensating transaction, bulkhead — and each pattern page carries the considerations that decide when it backfires. This lesson fits them to pipeline components.

item.title: Format-driven performance incidents — small scans and wrong layouts
item.description: When a scan reads the whole lake for one column, the cause is usually the file layout, not the engine — missing statistics, row groups sized without intent, encodings chosen by default. Walk two incident patterns grounded in what the Parquet sources actually claim about statistics and pruning.

item.title: Incident drill: a broken upstream caught by freshness and lineage
item.description: The source job quietly changed from hourly to daily; the mart's 6h freshness SLA now fails by construction. Run the drill — confirm the breach from the diff, walk upstream with get_lineage, and report the impact set with owner, criticality and the earliest SLA that breaks.

item.title: Instrument pipelines with OpenTelemetry: traces for data jobs
item.description: Traces give every pipeline run a story — which task ran, how long, with what attributes. Wrap a job with OpenTelemetry, adopt the semantic conventions so attribute names match across teams, and see exactly where runtime traces end and lineage events begin.

item.title: Lineage tooling in practice: DataHub MCP and the lineage-graph plugin
item.description: Put lineage to work with two tools — a DataHub MCP server that lets an agent search entities and read lineage and schema, and a lineage-graph plugin that turns column-level impact analysis into agent commands. Wire both, learn each tool surface, and scope the token before sharing it.

item.title: Production gotchas: alert fatigue, missing contracts, no-data silence
item.description: Three failure modes of a monitoring stack that looks healthy: alerts that page until nobody reads them, metrics with no declared SLA behind them, and no-data windows that pass as health. Grounded in the alerting semantics of Prometheus and Grafana and the schedule-vs-SLA contract.

item.title: Read reference architectures like an engineer — AWS as precedent
item.description: Reference architectures are precedent, not homework. This lesson teaches a reading method: name the moving parts, find the pillar each choice defends, spot the serverless data lake pattern, and re-state the diagram in DDIA vocabulary so vendor drawings become reusable design evidence.

item.title: Reading data files — from bytes to columnar memory
item.description: A read is a pipeline in miniature — the reader consults statistics, prunes row groups, decodes only the columns you asked for, and hands you an in-memory columnar structure. Walk the read path with the sources, then place it on the lifecycle between storage and transformation.

item.title: Speak the scaling vocabulary — load balancing, caching, sharding
item.description: Scale arguments go wrong when the words do: horizontal versus vertical, cache-aside versus write-through, shard by range versus hash. This lesson fixes the Primer's vocabulary and lines it up with DDIA's partitioning and replication so one argument covers both worlds.

item.title: Walkthrough: the lineage-explainer skill, from question to impact set
item.description: Install the lineage-explainer skill and walk it end to end: ask what breaks if a column changes, read technical and business lineage from the store, and produce an impact report with owner, criticality and the earliest SLA that breaks.

item.title: Capstone checklist — a design is done when these all hold
item.description: Nine lessons compress into one checklist: tradeoffs named, numbers written, storage chosen by mechanism, scaling lever identified, budget defined, failure patterns assigned, precedent cited. Run it on your next design and on the platform you already run.

item.title: Interview walkthrough — design a data platform end-to-end
item.description: The full arc in one 45-minute shape: requirements, back-of-envelope numbers, the storage and scaling argument, reliability as SLIs and budgets, and a deployed precedent to close. Every claim traces to one of the five sources, so nothing in the answer is invented under pressure.

item.title: Production gotchas — premature scaling and the missing capacity plan
item.description: The two self-inflicted design failures: complexity bought before load requires it, and capacity treated as an afterthought until the pager goes off. This lesson puts the SRE discipline of capacity planning next to the pattern catalogue's warnings, so design reviews catch both before production does.

item.title: First hands-on — a correct SELECT with a justified join
item.description: Stand up a local DuckDB through the DuckDB MCP server, inspect before you query with list_tables and describe_table, and write one SELECT with a join whose cardinality you can justify. You read CSV and Parquet straight into the engine, state the grain of the result, and finish by proving the join cannot fan out — the habit the sql-review skill demands.

item.title: Hold the cloud data stack mental model — storage, catalog, compute, IAM
item.description: Build the map before opening a console: object storage holds the bytes, a managed catalog describes them, and serverless compute bills for what a query scans. Walk the same shape through five managed engines — Glue, Athena, BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks — and note the IAM surface each one needs before the first query.

item.title: The data reliability mental model — freshness, completeness, correctness
item.description: Build the map before writing a single check: a consumer experiences a table as three properties — freshness, completeness, correctness — declared as an SLA in a data contract, enforced by a CI test, and spent like an error budget when failures land.

item.title: The lakehouse mental model — lake vs warehouse vs table formats vs zones
item.description: Build the map before touching a table: object storage is files with no structure for trust or ownership, a table format (Iceberg or Delta) adds snapshots, manifests, hidden partitioning, ACID, and evolution, and medallion zones make trust legible from raw to serving. Multi-catalog means the formats coexist — pick each one deliberately.

item.title: The orchestration mental model — DAGs, schedules, idempotency, backfills
item.description: Build the map before touching code: a DAG plus its schedule decides when runs happen, the idempotency test decides whether re-runs are safe, catchup decides what happens to missed intervals, and a backfill decides how history gets fixed — four decisions every later lesson sharpens.

item.title: The relational mental model — sets, grain, and NULL
item.description: Before the first SELECT, build the model every later lesson uses: a query returns a set with a stated grain, a join changes that grain by its cardinality, and NULL never compares as you expect. You learn the first question every SQL review asks, the five rules that follow from it, and the failure modes — fan-out joins, NULL-unsafe predicates, implicit casts, non-deterministic ordering, functions that silently change grain — the rest of the series attacks.

item.title: The warehouse mental model — micro-partitions, clustering, scan vs compute
item.description: Build the map before tuning anything: a table is a set of micro-partitions, every query is described by bytes scanned, partitions scanned ratio, and queue time, a clustering key decides how much gets pruned, and a slow query is either a scan problem or a compute problem — never both at once.

item.title: What makes an agent — model, tools, loop, guardrails
item.description: Build the map before touching anything: an agent is a model that reasons, tools that act, a loop that iterates, and guardrails that bound it. Meet a real data-engineering agent from the registry, point at each of the four parts, and see where the guardrails come from — hooks and the human gate.

item.title: Wire cloud tooling — registry skills, MCP servers, and one review workflow
item.description: Wire the registry's cloud tooling into one agent workflow: install the Glue and Athena review skills, bind the AWS MCP server to a least-privilege profile, and compose both skills plus the MCP server into the architecture reviewer. The same pattern covers GCP with the BigQuery server.

item.title: Your first lakehouse table — create, query, measure, compact
item.description: Run the whole loop in one sitting on a scratch table: create and query a first Delta or Iceberg table from the official docs, read its health from the files metadata table with one SQL query, run a first OPTIMIZE or rewrite_data_files, and prove it worked by comparing numFiles and bytes scanned before and after.

item.title: ACID and concurrent writes — why compaction and ingestion collide
item.description: What ACID on object storage actually guards, and where it stops: Delta commits transactions on files, but compaction is also a writer, and the two meet in the ingestion window. Learn the schedule rule, the write-path/layout-path separation, and how a guardrail blocks maintenance from running in the wrong window.

item.title: Capstone — the checklist that decides whether a DAG ships
item.description: Close the series by running the full review pass over your own pipeline: the idempotency test per task, partitioned or MERGE writes, deliberate catchup, backoff retries, reschedule sensors, bounded concurrency — and a documented runbook for the day history needs fixing.

item.title: Capstone — the cloud guardrail checklist
item.description: Close the series by turning nine lessons into one standing checklist: workgroup bytes limits and compaction on storage, sized workers and stable bookmarks on compute, resource monitors and unit-metric alerts on spend, and least-privilege IAM everywhere — then produce the four review outputs as evidence.

item.title: Capstone — the reliability checklist for a pipeline you can page on
item.description: Close the series by running the reliability checklist over your own pipeline: a declared and enforced SLA, idempotent tasks with backoff retries, a documented backfill runbook — then drill the incident path from alert to blameless postmortem with dated, owned action items.

item.title: Capstone — the SQL correctness checklist
item.description: Close the series by turning nine lessons into one standing checklist: a grain statement for every SELECT, a cardinality justification for every join, NULL-safe anti-joins, explicit casts, lint in CI, and one decision rule for slow queries. Each line cites the lesson that earned it, and the checklist ends where the review agent ends — with findings that cite severity, location, rule, and fix.

item.title: Capstone — the standing lakehouse checklist
item.description: Close the series by running the full checklist on one table you own: zones with gates, a deliberately chosen format, the three standing monitors, the four-part maintenance plan as a scheduled job, guardrail-enforced windows, and the escalation line that decides when it pages.

item.title: Capstone — the warehousing checklist, end to end
item.description: Close the series by auditing one warehouse project against everything it taught: models with tests and docs, layered staging to marts with a declared grain, incremental loads with a lookback, CI on a staging schema, monitored query history, and a repo structure a new joiner can read.

item.title: DR and replication — design the recovery path before you need it
item.description: Disaster recovery for data systems starts before the outage: DDIA's replication and consistency chapters name the mechanisms, and the registry's runbooks name the recovery paths — code rollback for deterministic failures, quarantine-then-retry for data errors, shadow-then-swap for recomputes.

item.title: Fan out over date batches with dynamic task mapping
item.description: Run one task definition over many date batches with dynamic task mapping — the docs' mapping feature applied the way the backfill material demands: batched ranges, smallest first, a validated sample after each batch.

item.title: Govern cloud spend — right-sizing, resource monitors, and unit economics
item.description: Govern cloud spend the way you govern data quality: right-size each warehouse per environment, put a resource monitor between the workload and the invoice, and alert on cost-per-run instead of total spend. Ends with the unit-economics rule that turns a 4x regression into a number, not a surprise.

item.title: Hooks — deterministic gates around an agent
item.description: The model can be talked into anything; a hook is code on the tool path. Walk the four safety hooks every data repo should know — destructive-SQL guard, prod write confirmation, secret scan, backfill safety check — and wire the two the starter plugin ships.

item.title: Idempotency and reruns — make every task safe to run twice
item.description: Retries are inevitable, so a task that appends duplicates rows every time it is cleared: hold each task to the idempotency test, replace its partition atomically instead of appending, and assert the invariant in CI with a test that runs the same date twice.

item.title: Incident — the dashboard query that went slow
item.description: Run the slow-query runbook as an incident: confirm the regression, split scan cost from compute contention, pull partitions_scanned and bytes from query history as evidence, apply the matched fix, and escalate on the shared-warehouse SLA before the queue takes other teams down with it.

item.title: Incident — the job that quadrupled in cost overnight
item.description: An invoice alert or a cost-per-run dashboard spike lands: one job's compute cost quadrupled with no functional change. Work the runbook — diff shuffle write and input bytes run-over-run, rank the four usual suspects, fix per cause, and cap the damage with a resource monitor while you diagnose.

item.title: Incident — the numbers doubled and no alarm fired
item.description: Row counts are inflated and metrics double-counted after a retry, a fan-out join or a backfill — the incident signature of a silent fan-out. You work the duplicate-records runbook end to end: count duplicates per key with one query, correlate the first duplicate date with a deploy, check whether the write is append or merge/overwrite, then dedupe on the business key and rewrite only the affected partitions.

item.title: Inside a skill — SKILL.md, references, examples, the loading protocol
item.description: A skill is the unit of reusable agent behavior: one SKILL.md with front-matter, plus directories the agent loads on demand. Dissect a real registry skill file by file, learn the evaluation rubric its objectives set, then install it and compare the layout with your own draft.

item.title: Make a DAG data-aware with reschedule-mode sensors
item.description: Stop guessing when upstream data arrives: add a sensor in reschedule mode so the DAG waits for its input without holding a worker slot, read the scheduling-semantics pages first, and bound the sensor with timeout and concurrency settings like any other task.

item.title: Make queries prune — clustering keys and scan diagnosis
item.description: Choose a clustering key from the predicates of your most expensive queries, prove the prune with partitions_scanned versus partitions_total, and fix the disease you actually have — a lost predicate or a low-selectivity key on the scan side, or queue time on the compute side.

item.title: Model a star schema — facts, conformed dimensions, declared grain
item.description: Turn the analytical layer into facts surrounded by conformed dimensions: declare the fact grain in schema.yml, stage and intermediate models below it, SCD2 where history must survive, and scaffold the whole thing from the dbt project template so staging, marts, tests, and CI exist from commit one.

item.title: Plan and execute a backfill that doesn't break production
item.description: Historical output is wrong or missing, and the fix touches a production table: define correct first, map the blast radius from lineage, then shadow-write in date batches smallest-first, validate a sample per batch, and swap atomically — behind a gate that demands a rollback path.

item.title: Production gotchas — NULL traps, implicit casts, silent drift
item.description: The bugs that survive testing compare wrong instead of failing loud: NOT IN over a nullable subquery, a comparison across types left to an implicit cast, and a schema change that silently turns a column to NULLs. You walk the review rules that ban each pattern, then use the schema-drift runbook to tell a hard failure from a silent one and to decide between an explicit cast and a quarantine.

item.title: Production gotchas — silent failures and partial writes
item.description: The failures that become pages are the ones nobody was watching: a regression hiding in growth, a cron change that silently widens the freshness SLA, and appends that duplicate on retry — cap each with a guard, a computed worst-case lag, and an atomic partition replace.

item.title: Production gotchas — surprise bills, region defaults, and IAM overreach
item.description: The surprises that turn into invoices: workers sized by habit, a renamed prefix that silently resets a bookmark, thousands of small files, an agent holding an admin role, and a query that scans everything because the predicate missed the partition column. Each gotcha names the metric that catches it early.

item.title: Production gotchas — topology, timeouts, concurrency
item.description: The DAG failures that become pages: unbounded concurrency, missing catchup policy, and a backfill that starves the daily run — cap them with max_active_runs and pools, then wire the monitoring and escalation path the backfill runbook prescribes.

item.title: Schema evolution and time travel — change the table, keep the past
item.description: Change a table without breaking its readers or its history: the Iceberg spec's schema and partition evolution, Delta time travel, the history metadata table you query to see what happened, and the snapshot-expiry rule that keeps time travel working while storage stays bounded. The immutable raw zone is the floor under all of it.

item.title: Table format mechanics — snapshots, manifests, and the metadata tables
item.description: Open the hood on an Iceberg table: the spec's layers (snapshots, manifests, hidden partitioning), the files and history metadata tables you query with plain SQL, and the manifest list as a maintenance target in its own right. One catalog then spans Iceberg, Delta, Hudi, and Hive.

item.title: Window functions — keep the grain, rank the rows
item.description: A window function computes over a set of rows and hands the answer back to every row, so the result keeps its grain — the property that makes a keep-latest dedupe safe and a bare GROUP BY grain-changing. You find the duplicates first with one GROUP BY query, dedupe on the business key keeping the latest by event time, and learn when a window over the same key is a shuffle that can skew or spill.

item.title: Wire task dependencies and retries that survive failure
item.description: Model the pipeline as task groups and give every task deliberate retries with backoff, a timeout and a pool — the skeleton's guarantees, verified the way the DAG reviewer verifies them before the DAG ships.

item.title: Capstone — the guarded agent checklist
item.description: Run the whole series against one agent setup: skills that load on demand, tools scoped at the connection, least-privilege credentials, audited tool contracts, hooks that fail closed, and a human gate on anything irreversible. Prove each box with an attempted violation, not a promise.

item.title: Production gotchas — untrusted content, destructive actions, permission scope
item.description: An agent executes with your credentials, so its context and config are an attack surface. Read the MCP security model, treat fetched content as untrusted input, keep destructive statements deny-by-default, and scope every credential to the role and repositories the task needs.

item.title: Warehouse production gotchas — cost, full refreshes, late data
item.description: The three ways a healthy warehouse model hurts production: a full-refresh that rebuilds a 4B-row table unannounced, a lookback window too short to catch late-arriving orders, and cost drift nobody reviews. Guard the destructive command, harden CI, and put the cost query on a weekly cadence.

item.title: When an agent does the wrong thing — contain, audit, postmortem
item.description: An agent merged a change it should not have. Roll back first, use the scoping you configured to contain and reconstruct what happened — diffs, logs and approve-once records — walk the incident workflow, and close with a blameless postmortem whose action items name the missing gate.

item.title: Apache Arrow Documentation
item.description: Official Arrow docs: the columnar in-memory format, its language bindings, IPC and Flight protocols, and zero-copy interchange between systems. Use it for exact memory-layout and type-system semantics behind every "columnar" claim in the registry.

item.title: Apache Avro Documentation
item.description: Avro's official documentation: schema declaration, the schema-registry evolution rules, encoding and the container format widely used for event/stream payloads and Kafka wire formats.

item.title: Apache Parquet Format Documentation
item.description: The Parquet file format documentation: page structure, encodings, compression codecs, statistics and the predicate-pushdown behavior that columnar readers rely on. The ground truth for why columnar files scan less data and how row-group pruning works.

item.title: AWS Architecture Center
item.description: AWS's official collection of architecture diagrams, reference architectures and best-practice guidance (Well-Architected pillars, serverless data lake patterns). Concrete vendor material for grounding sizing and tradeoff arguments in real deployed patterns.

item.title: Azure Cloud Design Patterns
item.description: Microsoft's catalogue of cloud design patterns: retry, circuit breaker, compensating transaction, CQRS, event sourcing, bulkhead and more — each with problem/solution and considerations. Vendor-neutral in practice, and directly applicable to pipeline component design.

item.title: Google SRE Books
item.description: Google's Site Reliability Engineering books, free online: SLIs/SLOs/error budgets, incident management, postmortem culture and capacity planning. The vocabulary source for reliability engineering that data platform teams borrow from when they define data SLAs and run incident drills.

item.title: Grafana Documentation
item.description: Grafana's official documentation: dashboards, panel queries, alerting (including the unified alerting model), and provisioning. The standard surface where pipeline freshness, volume and job-health dashboards live.

item.title: OpenTelemetry Documentation
item.description: OpenTelemetry's official documentation: traces, metrics and logs through a vendor-neutral API/SDK, the collector, and semantic conventions. Increasingly the default instrumentation layer for distributed pipelines and services.

item.title: PostgreSQL Documentation — Tutorial & Reference
item.description: PostgreSQL's official documentation: the tutorial, SQL reference, indexes, transactions and MVCC chapters. The semantics of transaction isolation and index behavior here are the ground truth for correctness arguments in pipeline source systems.

item.title: Prometheus Documentation
item.description: Official Prometheus docs: the pull-based metrics model, PromQL, exporters, service discovery and alerting rules. Data platforms lean on it for infrastructure- and job-level metrics that sit underneath data-quality signals like freshness and volume.

item.title: Python Official Documentation
item.description: The official Python 3 documentation: language reference, standard library (itertools, collections, dataclasses, json, csv), and the data-model chapter that explains iteration, mutability and hashing semantics every data script depends on.

item.title: SQLBolt — Learn SQL with Simple Interactive Exercises
item.description: Free interactive SQL lessons: SELECT basics, filtering, joins, NULL handling and aggregate clauses, each runnable in the browser. A zero-setup first step before touching a real warehouse or local DuckDB.

item.title: The System Design Primer
item.description: The widely-used open-source study guide for system design: scaling vocabulary (load balancers, caching, sharding), back-of-envelope estimation, and worked design exercises. Data platform architectures are a special case of the same throughput/consistency tradeoffs it teaches.

item.title: The Twelve-Factor App
item.description: The classic twelve principles for building services that run portably: config in the environment, backing services as attached resources, logs as event streams, disposability and dev/prod parity. Data pipelines inherit these ideas whenever they run as jobs on shared infrastructure.

item.title: Author your first data contract
item.description: Draft an enforceable contract for one real dataset by walking the six parts — owner, schema, semantics, SLA, breaking-change policy, enforcement — starting from the data-contract template, and finish with the CI test that makes it a contract instead of documentation.

item.title: Compute unit economics for a pipeline
item.description: Turn cluster and warehouse billing into unit economics — cost per run, per 1M rows, per model build — so a regression shows up as a number, not a surprise invoice. The Cost Optimizer starts with attribution; this walkthrough ends with an alert on cost-per-run instead of total spend.

item.title: Cut Athena bytes scanned with partitions and projection
item.description: Walk one expensive Athena query through the Partition Advisor's levers in order: confirm the per-TB bill model, partition on the dominant filter column, replace MSCK REPAIR with partition projection, compact small files, and move to columnar compression. Every move is judged by a single number — bytes scanned.

item.title: Decide when a Delta table needs OPTIMIZE or Z-ORDER
item.description: Apply the Delta Optimization Advisor's decision rules to one table: read file stats for the OPTIMIZE trigger, pick Z-ORDER columns from actual query predicates, weigh liquid clustering for high-cardinality write-heavy tables, and prove the choice by comparing numFiles and bytes scanned before and after.

item.title: Deduplicate records without rewriting the table
item.description: Row counts are inflated and revenue double-counted after a retry or a fan-out join. Work the duplicate-records runbook: find the first duplicate date, correlate it with a deploy, dedupe on the business key, and rewrite only the affected partitions.

item.title: Enforce contracts in CI with the schema change check
item.description: Install the Schema Change Check as a pre-commit gate over staged schema files so a breaking change exits non-zero unless a migration plan or deprecation annotation rides along with it — the producer-CI placement that catches breakage before merge.

item.title: Fix SQL lint with the SQLFluff core rule pack
item.description: Install the SQLFluff core rule pack, point it at your warehouse dialect, and lint a fixture that fails on purpose: indentation, keyword capitalisation, SELECT star, and unused CTEs. You fix each finding while the passing fixture stays green, then wire the same lint run into CI.

item.title: Hold the streaming mental model: events, partitions, delivery semantics
item.description: Build the vocabulary before touching a cluster: events instead of rows, partitions instead of tables, at-least-once delivery instead of exactly-once, and the lambda/kappa decision for speed versus correctness. Every later lesson in this series leans on these four ideas.

item.title: Inspect Kafka topics and groups with the Kafka MCP server
item.description: Connect an agent to a Kafka cluster through the Kafka MCP server and work through its four tools: list_topics for inventory, describe_topic for a single topic, describe_consumer_group for lag, and consume_messages for sampling — stream debugging from an agent, with the sampling risks called out up front.

item.title: Install cost guardrails before the invoice
item.description: Instrument, attribute, then guard: the Cost Guardrails pattern in four moves — a unit metric per pipeline, a baseline of the last N runs, CI failing on regression, and hard caps. It ends with a build that fails on a 3.9x shuffle jump instead of a surprise invoice.

item.title: Keep an agent read-only until a human approves
item.description: Coding agents can do real data-engineering work, but can also ship a schema change or drop a table. Walk the Agent-in-the-Loop Review pattern: separate read/recommend from write/execute, put a human gate before anything irreversible, and encode the policy as hooks.

item.title: Name the four dimensions of data quality
item.description: Build the mental model before writing a single test: freshness, completeness, validity, consistency. See each dimension in a real registry artifact — the SLA part of a contract, the profiling workflow of the data-quality reviewer, the rule vocabulary of the quarantine starter — and leave able to name the dimension behind any "the data is bad" complaint.

item.title: Respond to a failing quality expectation
item.description: A quality expectation failed in production and bad data may be reaching consumers. Follow the data-quality-failure runbook: read the failure precisely, quantify it, then make the one decision that matters — block, quarantine, or pass-with-warning.

item.title: Review a DAG for idempotency and retry safety
item.description: Walk the Pipeline Reviewer's four-step pass over a DAG: apply the idempotency test to every task, check retry, timeout and concurrency settings, predict backfill behaviour, and propose missing integration tests — then close the loop with the Airflow DAG Reviewer's checklist so every task is safe to re-run before the DAG merges.

item.title: Review a Glue job for sizing, bookmarks, and catalogue drift
item.description: Take a Glue/Spark job through the AWS Glue Job Reviewer's three checks: size workers from the input files' partitions instead of habit, verify the job bookmark against the input path layout, and diff the Glue Data Catalog schema against the Parquet file footer. Each check targets a silent cost leak that ends in full reprocessing.

item.title: Run the dbt warehouse tests starter end to end
item.description: Clone the dbt-warehouse-tests starter, seed its deterministic customers and orders data, and build the staging → intermediate → marts pipeline with dbt build --target dev. You serve the docs, add the tests that protect the fct grain, and finish against the failure scenarios the project warns about.

item.title: Run the full SQL review pass on a PR
item.description: Run the SQL Reviewer agent's full pass over a pull request: read the diff in context, state the grain of every result set, then check the correctness bugs the SQL Review skill targets — fan-out joins, NULL-unsafe NOT IN and = predicates — and emit findings with file:line and a rewritten clause you can verify against the evaluation fixture.

item.title: Scaffold an idempotent DAG from the template
item.description: Generate a new pipeline from the Airflow DAG template and keep its guarantees — an idempotent skeleton with task groups, retries and backoff, SLA, pools, and a reschedule-mode sensor — then make catchup a deliberate choice and every write partition-keyed or a MERGE.

item.title: Stand up the S3 → Glue → Athena starter
item.description: Deploy the serverless query-in-place starter end to end: Terraform provisions buckets, catalog, and a bounded Athena workgroup, Parquet lands in a Hive layout, the table is registered with partition projection, and pruning is proven with explain analyze. The sample data ships one deliberately oversized file to demonstrate compaction.

item.title: Start a PySpark project from the template
item.description: Scaffold a testable PySpark project with one command and learn where each piece lives: transforms in src/, 3-10 row fixtures in tests/data/, and a Makefile that runs lint plus tests offline. Finish by hardening the first transform with row-count and null assertions.

item.title: The batch processing mental model
item.description: Batch processing in partition terms. Learn what a partition, a shuffle and a spill are, why "the job is slow" resolves into four named causes — skew, partition count, spill, over-scan — and why the write side carries one invariant: same date twice, same output.

item.title: Troubleshoot a lagging group with the Kafka Troubleshooter
item.description: Hand the Kafka Troubleshooter agent the consumer-group describe output, per-partition offsets, and consumer logs, then follow its four-step workflow from lag trend to the least destructive fix. The agent works read-only against the cluster, never resets offsets, and ships every fix with a risk rating.

item.title: Wire the core MCP servers for a data repo
item.description: Wire the three reference MCP servers a data repo needs: filesystem for the working directory, git for history and commits, and GitHub for issues and pull requests. Each connection is scoped — one directory, one repository, one fine-grained token.

item.title: Write the minimum dbt test set for a model
item.description: Start from the model's grain, then rank dbt tests by the cost of the failure they prevent: uniqueness and not-null on the grain key, relationships on foreign keys, accepted values on enums, and freshness on sources. You add one custom singular test, wire freshness on a source, and finish by running the set in data-aware CI against a staging schema.

item.title: Aggregations and windows without the skew
item.description: Aggregations and windows are shuffles in disguise. Treat the group-by key as a skew suspect, read p50 vs p99 and the spill bytes, then apply the matching fix — a salted two-stage aggregate, more partitions, or a partition predicate — and never repartition(1).

item.title: Attribute a 4x Spark cost regression
item.description: One job's compute cost quadrupled overnight with no functional change. Run the 4x runbook: diff shuffle and input bytes run-over-run, find the guilty stage, reverse the regression — then wire hook-spark-cost-check so the next one fails CI before the invoice.

item.title: Attribute spend with the Cost Lens plugin
item.description: Install the Cost Lens plugin and use its three commands to attribute spend, compute unit economics, and guard cost-per-run. The plugin pairs the unit-economics skill with the Spark cost regression guard, and ships the hooks that enforce the guard in CI.

item.title: Audit an MCP server's tool contracts
item.description: Before connecting an MCP server, audit its tools for blast radius. Read each tool schema, classify every tool as Read, Write, Destructive, Spend or Exfiltrate, and produce a least-privilege connection config that grants only what the task needs.

item.title: Capstone — the batch pipeline checklist
item.description: Bring the API → S3 → Spark → Parquet starter up end to end, then audit it: offline transform tests, idempotent partition-scoped writes, complete partitions, replay-safe extraction, and baseline metrics with a CI guard. One pipeline that exercises every lesson in the series.

item.title: Capstone — wire a dataset's quality gates end to end
item.description: Close the series by walking one SLA-bearing dataset through every gate the series taught — six-part contract, CI compatibility check, staged quality suite, quarantine split, quarantine-rate alerts — and finish with the monitoring signals and incident paths that keep the gates honest.

item.title: Check lakehouse table health with Lakehouse Guard
item.description: Use the Lakehouse Guard plugin's three commands on a Delta/Iceberg table: /table-health for a status read, /plan-compaction for a maintenance plan, and /expire-snapshots for a safe expiry plan. The guard exists to block compaction or snapshot expiry during peak ingestion windows, so plans cannot run in the wrong window.

item.title: Debug a Kafka stream with the Kafka Console plugin
item.description: Drive the Kafka Console plugin's three commands across a lag incident: /topic-info for inventory, /lag-triage for per-partition lag and rebalance detection, and /sample-topic for a read-only message sample with a PII redaction pass. Permissions stay at kafka-sasl-read throughout.

item.title: Diagnose a skewed Spark stage
item.description: One Spark stage hangs while other executors idle. Open the stage view, read the p50-vs-p99 task durations, and follow the skew skill's decision order: AQE skew join first, salting second, broadcast only under a size budget — and never repartition(1).

item.title: Diagnose a small-files explosion
item.description: Follow the small-files runbook from symptom to prevention: confirm the tens-of-thousands-of-tiny-files signature, query the metadata tables for the average file size, compact to a 128-256 MB target, coarsen an over-partitioned layout, and schedule compaction outside the ingestion window. The fix follows the small-files compaction pattern — separate the write path from the layout path.

item.title: Gate backfills with the safety check hook
item.description: Wire the Backfill Safety Check as a pre-run gate that refuses any backfill lacking an explicit date range, a shadow or snapshotted target, and a window clear of the scheduled production run — and watch it block the bare backfill command that would otherwise corrupt the target.

item.title: Gate promotion with a pre-deploy DQ check
item.description: Wire the pre-deployment DQ check so a pipeline is only promoted when its quality suite passes against staged output. You attach the pre-deploy trigger, run dbt/GE tests on the staging namespace, and prove a failed expectation leaves production untouched.

item.title: Incremental processing with a watermark
item.description: Full reloads stop scaling once a table grows past millions of rows. Process a bounded window instead: a watermark ends it, a lookback absorbs late files, and an idempotent write (partition overwrite or MERGE) makes every re-run safe — including re-processing a late window.

item.title: Make the sink idempotent so replays never duplicate rows
item.description: The core producer-side reliability skill for streams: you cannot stop replays, so the sink must converge. Deduplicate by a business key and event time within the watermark, MERGE on the key, and rank change events by (lsn, ts_ms) — never by arrival time.

item.title: Onboard an agent with the DE Data Toolkit
item.description: Onboard an agent onto a data repo with the DE Data Toolkit plugin: the SQL/Spark review skills, the destructive-SQL guard, a secret scanner, and the file/git MCP servers already wired. Learn the three commands and which hooks run underneath.

item.title: Own the consumer side — offsets, rebalances, and the KIP-848 protocol
item.description: Consumer reliability is where streams quietly break: a rebalance loop looks like slowness, consumers past the partition count buy nothing, and stop-the-world rebalances pause consumption. Read group state, fix the timeouts, and know what the next-generation protocol changes.

item.title: Plan and execute a safe backfill
item.description: Use the Backfill Planner's four-step plan — correctness criteria, downstream impact from lineage, cost and contention, staged batches — then execute it the way the backfill runbook demands: shadow table, sample validation per batch, and never beside the daily production run.

item.title: Production gotchas — the configs and capacities that break streams
item.description: The five causes of consumer lag on one card, the two destructive shortcuts that must never happen, and the capacity trap of scaling past the partition count. Ends with the alert that matters — lag slope, not absolute lag — and the sampling rules that keep PII out of agent contexts.

item.title: Read a Spark event log with the Spark Lens plugin
item.description: Install the Spark Lens plugin and work its three commands over a Spark event log: /spark-analyze to build a task histogram and flag skew, /spark-explain-plan to check the join strategy, and /spark-baseline to store the cost baseline the guard enforces.

item.title: Read an EXPLAIN plan and pick the one fix
item.description: Take the EXPLAIN output of a slow query and read it bottom-up, naming the expensive node before you touch anything. You compare estimated rows to actual rows to catch stale statistics, separate scan cost from compute time with the warehouse runbook, and finish by deciding between an index, a rewrite, or a stats refresh — one change, with a way to measure it.

item.title: Respond when a data contract breaks
item.description: Work the broken-contract runbook end to end: identify which clause broke, bound the consumer impact set from lineage before anything else, decide whether the producer reverts or the consumer adapts, and close with consumer-driven contract tests in the producer's pipeline.

item.title: Review a dbt model PR before merge
item.description: Take a pull request that adds or changes a dbt model and walk the reviewer's pass: read the diff in context, state the model's grain and check it against the unique key test, choose table vs incremental vs view deliberately, and handle late-arriving data in the incremental filter. You finish with findings a reviewer can verify before the model merges.

item.title: Review a PySpark transform for silent quality failures
item.description: Run the five-check pass over a PySpark transform before it merges: null propagation, join fan-out, silent coercion, non-determinism, and missing post-write assertions. Each finding lands as severity, file:line, rule and a suggested patch.

item.title: Review a schema change against its contract
item.description: Run the Schema Reviewer's four-step pass over a producer's schema diff — classify each field change, resolve consumers from lineage, emit a dated migration plan — and use the schema-drift runbook to separate hard failures from silent nulls before anything merges.

item.title: Run an AWS data architecture review pass
item.description: Point the AWS Architecture Reviewer at an architecture description or IaC and follow its four-step workflow: map the services to a data flow, check IAM for least privilege, estimate dominant cost drivers, and identify single points of failure. The agent is read-only and never creates resources.

item.title: Run dbt model review and tests from the workbench plugin
item.description: Install the dbt Workbench plugin and drive one model change through its three commands: /dbt-review-model for the model review, /dbt-write-tests for a proposed test set, and /dbt-impact before you merge. Along the way you apply the same grain and blast-radius checks the plugin's underlying skills use, with the full-refresh guard watching destructive rebuilds.

item.title: Run the Iceberg maintenance routine
item.description: Work an Iceberg table through the maintenance skill's plan: read the files metadata table to size the problem, rewrite data files to a 128-256 MB target, rewrite manifests when the manifest list is huge, expire snapshots without breaking time travel, and remove orphan files on a schedule with a safety margin.

item.title: Split a batch into quarantine and publish
item.description: Build the pipeline-dq-quarantine starter the way the Quarantine then Publish pattern prescribes: a quality contract splits each batch into a published set and a quarantine with reasons. You finish with a test that proves no row is ever lost and an alert on the quarantine rate.

item.title: Stream changes, not tables — CDC from Postgres into the lakehouse
item.description: The intermediate pattern that replaces nightly extraction: read the write-ahead log through Debezium, stream through Kafka, dedupe by LSN, and MERGE into Delta/Iceberg. Covers tombstones, decimal handling, and what a dropped replication slot costs you.

item.title: Triage Kafka consumer lag from per-partition offsets
item.description: Combine the lag-triage skill's three questions with the lagging-consumer runbook: read per-partition lag to separate capacity from key skew, check the group state history for a rebalance loop, find the one stuck offset that marks a poison message, then apply the matching fix — and never reset offsets.

item.title: Window a stream correctly — watermarks, dedupe, and late data
item.description: Stream processing in practice: start from the kafka-streaming template, pick event-time over processing-time windows, set a watermark you can defend, and prove what happens to late data. Checkpointing and an idempotent MERGE sink make the job restartable without duplicating output.

item.title: The 3am batch incident path
item.description: The nightly job is crawling or dead under memory pressure or skew. Follow the incident path: collect the four pieces of evidence, read p50 vs p99 and the spill bytes, decide revert vs fix, escalate on golden-hour SLAs, and record the skew/spill/scan signature so the next run is faster to diagnose.
